title: Security
description: Understanding how systems are attacked in order to build and defend them: web and API security, identity, cryptography, networks, cloud, secure development, and detection.

subdomains.title: Security Testing in Labs
examples: Intercepting traffic with Burp Suite or ZAP
Privilege escalation in a lab VM

default_stack.runtime: Python 3.11+ with Docker for isolated lab targets

safety: Authorized targets only: the learner's own machines, local containers and VMs, intentionally vulnerable apps (OWASP Juice Shop, DVWA, WebGoat, crAPI), and training platforms (PortSwigger Web Security Academy, Hack The Box, TryHackMe, OverTheWire, picoCTF).
Never scan, probe, or attack real third-party systems, networks, accounts, or people, including "just to check". Example commands always use localhost, 127.0.0.1, or a named lab container.
Run vulnerable apps bound to 127.0.0.1 on an isolated Docker network; never expose them to the internet or a shared network; remove them after the lab.
Defensive framing: every attack technique is taught together with how to detect it and how to fix it, and every exploit exercise ends with the patch and a regression test.
Do not write or keep malware, ransomware, credential stealers, phishing kits, or tools built to evade detection on real systems.
Never use real leaked credentials, real personal data, or real breach dumps; use generated test data.
Bug bounty work is done only inside a program's published scope and rules; when in doubt, do not test.
A vulnerability found by accident in a real product is reported privately to the vendor (coordinated disclosure), never exploited or published first.
Never commit secrets: API keys, tokens, and passwords live in a git-ignored .env file, with a committed .env.example that holds placeholder values only.
